la:verb:adduco.gloss: to lead, bring, draw or convey to or to oneself
senses: to lead, bring, draw or convey to or to oneself
to prompt, induce, cause
to persuade, move
to wrinkle, contract, shrink
to tighten or pull tight; (also) to contract
la:verb:adduco.html:
ad-dūco, xi, ctum, 3, v. a. (adduce for adduc, ; ; Afr. ap. :
adduxti for adduxisti,; : adduxe = adduxisse,), to lead to, to bring or convey to, draw to any place or to one's self (opp. abduco, q. v.; syn.: adfero, apporto, adveho, induco).
Lit.: quaeso, quī possim animum bonum habere, qui te ad me adducam domum,: ille alter venit, quem secum adduxit Parmenio,; Afr. ap. : quos secum Mitylenis Cratippus adduxit, Cic. Fil. ap. : Demetrius Epimachum secum adduxit,.—With ad: ad lenam,; cf. : ad cenam, Lucil. ap. (cf.: abduxi ad cenam,

9): adduxit ea ad Adam,; .—Or with a local adv.: tu istos adduce intro,: quia te adducturam huc dixeras eumpse non eampse,; so : adduc huc filium tuum,. —

In gen., without regard to the access. idea of accompanying, to lead or bring a person or thing to a place, to take or conduct from one place to another (of living beings which have the power of motion, while affero is properly used of things: attuli hunc. Pseud. Quid? attulisti? Ca. Adduxi volui dicere, ).—So of conducting an army: exercitum,: aquam,to lead to,.—With in: gentes feras in Italiam,; cf. Oud. ad , and Auct. B. G. 8, 35: in judicium adductus,: adducta res in judicium est,; so .—With dat.: puero nutricem adducit,: qui ex Gallia pueros venales isti adducebat,.—Poet. with acc.: Diae telluris ad oras applicor et dextris adducor litora remis, (cf. advertor oras Scythicas, , and Rudd. II. p. 327): adducere ad populum, i. e. in judicium populi vocare,.—Of a courtesan, to procure: puero scorta,: paelicem,.—Poet. also of a place, which is, as it were, brought near. Thus Hor. in describing the attractions of his Sabine farm: dicas adductum propius frondere Tarentum, Ep. 1, 16, 11.—
Esp.
To bring a thing to a destined place by drawing or pulling, to draw or pull to one's self: tormenta eo graviores emissiones habent, quo sunt contenta atque adducta vehementius,: adducto arcu,; so, adducta sagitta,: utque volat moles, adducto concita nervo,: adducta funibus arbor corruit,: funem,: so : colla parvis lacertis,: equos,.—Hence trop.: habenas amicitiae,to tighten,; cf. , and 1, 63.—
Of the skin or a part of the body, to draw up, wrinkle, contract: adducit cutem macies,wrinkles the skin,: sitis miseros adduxerat artus,; so, frontem (opp. remittere), to contract: interrogavit, quae causa frontis tam adductae?a brow so clouded?; so .
Fig.
To bring a person or thing into a certain condition; with ad or in: numquam animum quaesti gratiā ad malas adducam partīs,: rem adduci ad interregnum,: ad arbitrium alterius,: ad suam auctoritatem,: numquam prius discessit, quam ad finem sermo esset adductus,: iambos ad umbilicum adducere,: in discrimen extremum,; cf. : in summas angustias,: in invidiam falso crimine,: in necessitatem,: vitam in extremum,.—
To bring or lead one to a certain act, feeling, or opinion; to prompt, induce, prevail upon, persuade, move, incite to it; with ad, in, or ut (very freq. and class., and for the most part in a good sense; while seducere and inducere denote instigating or seducing to something bad, Herz. ; although there are exceptions, as the foll. examples show): ad misericordiam,: ad nequitiem,: ad iracundiam, ad fletum,: quae causa ad facinus adduxit,: in metum,: in summam exspectationem,: in spem,: in opinionem,: in suspicionem alicui,: ad paenitentiam,; .—With gerund: ad suspicandum,: ad credendum,.—With ut: adductus sum officio, fide, misericordia, etc., ut onus hoc laboris mihi suscipiendum putarem,: nullo imbre, nullo frigore adduci, ut capite operto sit,: ; ; , etc.; ; —And absol. in pass.: quibus rebus adductus ad causam accesserim demonstravi,: his rebus adducti,being induced,; .—With quin: adduci nequeo quin existimem,.—With inf.: facilius adducor ferre humana humanitus, Afr. ap. .—
Adducor with inf., or with ut and subj. = adducor ad credendum, πείθομαι, to be induced to believe: ego non adducor, quemquam bonum ullam salutem putare mihi tanti fuisse,: ut jam videar adduci, hanc quoque, quae te procrearit, esse patriam,: illud adduci vix possum, ut ... videantur,; ; .—Hence, adductus, a, um, P. a.
Drawn tight, stretched, strained, contracted.—Trop.: vultus,: frons in supercilia adductior,; cf. .—Hence,
Of place, narrow, contracted, strait: (Africa) ex spatio paulatim adductior,.—
Of character, strict, serious, severe: modo familiaritate juvenili Nero et rursus adductus, quasi seria consociaret,: adductum et quasi virile servitium,: vis pressior et adductior,.—Sup. not used.—Adv. only in comp.adductĭus,
More tightly: adductius contorquere jacula,.—
Trop., more strictly: imperitare,: regnari,.

senses: to add
to put, place, lay a person or thing to another
to acquire
to give, bring, add, or contribute to; annex, augment
la:verb:addo.html:
ad-do, dĭdi, dĭtum, 3, v. a.
2. do
(addues for addideris, Paul. ex Müll.),
to put, place, lay, etc., a person or thing to another.
In gen.
Lit., NEVE AVROM ADDITO, let no gold be put into the grave with the dead, Fragm. of the XII. Tab. in : Argus, quem quondam Ioni Juno custodem addidit, Plaut. Aul. 3, 6, 20; so : adimunt diviti, addunt pauperi,: spumantia addit Frena feris,: Pergamaque Iliacamque jugis hanc addidit arcem, i.e. imposuit,; : flammae aquam,to throw upon,: incendia ramis,: propiorem Martem,to bring nearer,.— With in: uram in ollulas addere,: glandem in dolium,: eas epistulas in eundem fasciculum velim addas,: adde manus in vincla meas,; .—Poet.: cum carceribus sese effudere quadrigae, addunt in spatia, i. e. dant se,, v. Heyne and Forb.—Hence,
Trop., to bring to, to add to; with dat.: pudicitiae hujus vitium me hinc absente'st additum,: fletum ingenio muliebri, Pac. ap. ; also absol.: operam addam sedulo,; so : addere animum, or animos, to give courage, make courageous: mihi quidem addit animum,: sed haec sunt in iis libris, quos tu laudando animos mihi addidisti,; so, animos cum clamore,.—So also: addis mihi alacritatem scribendi,: verba virtutem non addere,impart, bestow,: severitas dignitatem addiderat,: audaciam,: formidinem,: metum,; cf. : ex ingenio suo quisque demat vel addat fidem,: ardorem mentibus,: ductoribus honores,; hence, addere alicui calcar, to give one the spur, to spur him on: anticipate atque addite calcar, Varr. ap. : vatibus addere calcar, (cf.: admovere calcar , and adhibere calcar, ).
Esp.
To add to by way of increase, to join or annex to, to augment, with dat. or ad (the most common signif. of this word): etiam fides, ei quae accessere, tibi addam dono gratiis,: verbum adde etiam unum,; cf. : non satis habes quod tibi dieculam addo?; so ; : illud in his rebus non addunt,: quaeso ne ad malum hoc addas malum, Caec. ap. : addendo deducendoque videre quae reliqui summa fiat,; so ; ; id : acervum efficiunt uno addito grano,: hunc laborem ad cotidiana opera addebant,: multas res novas in edictum addidit,he made essential additions to,: eaque res multum animis eorum addidit,: addita est alia insuper injuria,: novas litterarum formas addidit vulgavitque,; cf. —Poet.: noctem addens operi,also the night to the work,; ut quantum generi demas, virtutibus addas,.— With ad: additum ad caput legis,; so .—Poet. with inf.: ille viris pila et ferro circumdare pectus addiderat,he instructed them in addition,: addere gradum (sc. gradui), to add step to step, i. e. to quicken one's pace: adde gradum, appropera,; so ; ; ; cf. Doed. Syn. 4, 58: addito tempore, in course of time: conjugia sobrinarum diu ignorata addito tempore percrebuisse,; so also: addita aetate, with increased age: in infantia scabunt aures; quod addita aetate non queunt,as they grow older,.—
Mercant. t. t., to add to one's bidding, to give more: nihil addo, Poët. ap. .—
When a new thought is added to what precedes, as an enlargement of it, it is introduced by adde, adde huc, adde quod, and the like (cf. accedo), add to this, add to this the circumstance that, or besides, moreover . . .: adde furorem animi proprium atque oblivia rerum, adde quod in nigras lethargi mergitur undas, (cf. the third verse before: advenit id quod eam de rebus saepe futuris Macerat): adde huc, si placet, unguentarios, saltatores totumque ludum talarium,: adde hos praeterea casus, etc.,: adde huc populationem agrorum,: adde quod pubes tibi crescit omnis, Hor. C. 2, 8, 17; : adde quod ingenuas didicisse fideliter artes Emollit mores nec sinit esse feros,: adde huc quod mercem sine fucis gestat,: adde super dictis quod non levius valeat,.—So also when several are addressed, as in the speech of Scipic to his soldiers: adde defectionem Italiae, Siciliae, etc.,.—Also with the acc. and inf.: addebat etiam, se in legem Voconiam juratum contra eam facere non audere,; and with an anticipatory dem. pron.: Addit etiam illud, equites non optimos fuisse,: Addit haec, fortes viros sequi, etc.,: addito as abl. absol. with a subj. clause; with the addition, with this addition (post-Aug.): vocantur patres, addito consultandum super re magna et atroci, with this intimation, that they were to consult, etc., : addito ut luna infra terram sit, (cf.: adjuncto ut ... haberentur,).— Hence, addĭtus, a, um, P. a. (addo I.), joined to one as a constant observer; so,
Watching or observing in a hostile or troublesome manner: si mihi non praetor siet additus atque agitet me, Lucil. ap. .—Hence, in gen.,
Pursuing one incessantly, persecuting: nec Teucris addita Juno Usquam aberit, Serv. (= adfixa, incumbens, infesta).

la:verb:addubito.gloss: to incline to doubt, begin to doubt, feel doubt, be uncertain
senses: to incline to doubt, begin to doubt, feel doubt, be uncertain
to be doubtful of (something), call in question
to hesitate
la:verb:addubito.html:
ad-dŭbĭto, āvi, ātum, 1, v. n. and a.
, pr., to incline to doubt, to begin to doubt (in Cic. several times, but never in his orations).
To be in doubt, to doubt; constr.
With de or in aliqua re: de quo Panaetium addubitare dicebant,: de legatis paululum addubitatum est,: in his addubitare turpissimum est,.—
With pron., or num, an, etc.: ut addubitet, quid potius dicat,: addubitavi, num a Volumnio senatore esset,: an hoc inhonestum necne sit, addubites,; so ; cf. Drak. ad : illud addubitat, utrum, etc., (acc. to Br. ad h. l.: to leave it undecided; cf. with dubitare, ).—
With acc., to be doubtful of a thing, to call in question: si plus adipiscare, re explicata, boni, quam addubitata mali,; so .—
With inf., to hesitate: aptare lacertos addubitat,.—(ε) Absol.: eos ipsos addubitare coget doctissimorum hominum tanta dissentio,; ; .
la:verb:addubito.inflection: āvi, ātum, 1, v. n. and a.

la:verb:addico.gloss: to be propitious to, favour, speak favourably (of)
senses: to be propitious to, favour, speak favourably (of)
to attribute, assign or ascribe something to someone; appoint, designate; award; sentence, condemn
to deliver, yield, or resign something to someone; give up, abandon, surrender; betray; enslave (to)
to devote, consecrate to, give one's support to, sacrifice
to adjudge to the highest bidder, knock down (to), strike off, deliver to
to sell
la:verb:addico.html:
ad-dīco, xi, ctum, 3, v. a. (
imp. addice, for addic, ; addixti,), orig., to give one's assent to a thing (addicere est proprie idem dicere et approbare dicendo, Müll.), in its lit. signif. belonging only to augural and judicial language (opp. abdĭco).
Of a favorable omen, to be propitious to, to favor, usually with aves as subj., and without obj.: cum sacellorum exaugurationes admitterent aves, in Termini fano non addixere,; so, Fabio auspicanti aves semel atque iterum non addixerunt,; also with auspicium as subj.: addicentibus auspiciis vocat contionem,; cf. Drak. ; .—And with acc. of obj.: illum quem aves addixerant, Müll.—In judicial lang.: alicui aliquid or aliquem, to award or adjudge any thing to one, to sentence; hence Festus, with reference to the adjudged or condemned person, says: alias addicere damnare est, p. 13 Müll.: ubi in jus venerit, addicet praetor familiam totam tibi,: bona alicui,: addictus erat tibi?had he been declared bound to you for payment?; hence ironic.: Fufidium . . . creditorem debitoribus suis addixisti, you have adjudged the creditor to his debtors (instead of the reverse), : liberum corpus in servitutem,.—Hence subst., addictus, i, m., one who has been given up or made over as servant to his creditor: ducite nos quo jubet, tamquam quidem addictos,: addictus Hermippo et ab hoc ductus est,extr.; cf. . (The addictus, bondman, was not properly a slave = servus, for he retained his nomen, cognomen, his tribus, which the servus did not have; he could become free again by cancelling the demand, even against the will of his dominus; the servus could not; the addictus, when set free, was also again ingenuus, the servus only libertinus; v. . The inhuman law of the Twelve Tables, which, however, was never put in execution, that one indebted to several creditors should be cut in pieces and divided among them, is mentioned by : Niebuhr, Rom. Gesch. 1, 638; Smith's Antiq.): addicere alicui judicium,to grant one leave to bring an action, Müll.: addicere litem, sc. judici, to deliver a cause to the judge. This was the office of the praetor. Such is the purport of the law of XII. Tab. Tab. I.: POST MERIDIEM PRAESENTI STLITEM ADDICITO, ap. : judicem or arbitrum (instead of dare judicium),to appoint for one a judge in his suit, and 80: addicere aliquid in diem, to adjudge a thing to one ad interim, so that, upon a change of circumstances, the matter in question shall be restored in integrum, ; ; .—
In auctions, to adjudge to the highest bidder, knock down, strike off, deliver to (with the price in abl.): ecquis est ex tanto populo, qui bona C. Rabirii Postumi

nummo sestertio sibi addici velit, ; so ; .—Addicere bona alicujus in publicum, i. e. to confiscate, ; hence in Plaut., of a parasite, who strikes himself off, as it were, i. e. promises himself to one as guest, on condition that he does not in the mean time have a higher bid, i. e. is not attracted to another by a better table,—

In gen., to sell, to make over to: addice tuam mihi meretricem,: hominem invenire neminem potuit, cui meas aedes addiceret, traderet, donaret, Auct. Or. pro Dom. 41. Antonius regna addixit pecunia,; so .—In a metaph. signif.,
To deliver, yield, or resign a thing to one, either in a good or a bad sense.
In a good sense, to devote, to consecrate to: senatus, cui me semper addixi,: agros omnes addixit deae,; hence, morti addicere,to devote to death,: nolite . . . omnem Galliam prosternere et perpetuae servituti addicere,to devote to perpetual slavery,.—
In a bad sense, to give up, to sacrifice, to abandon (very freq.); ejus ipsius domum evertisti, cujus sanguinem addixeras,: libidini cujusque nos addixit,; so ; ; ; hence poet.: quid faciat? crudele, suos addicere amores,to sacrifice, to surrender his love, (where some read wrongly abdicere).—
In later Latin, to attribute or ascribe a work to one: quae (comoediae) nomini eius (Plauti) addicuntur,.—Hence, addic-tus, P. a. (after II. D.), dedicated or devoted to a thing; hence,
Destined to: gladiatorio generi mortis addictus,; cf. .—
Given up to, bound to: qui certis quibusdam destinatisque sententiis quasi addicti et consecrati sunt,: nullius addictus jurare in verba magistri,: Prasinae factioni addictus et deditus,.—Comp., sup., and adv. not used.

In gen., to learn, to be informed, to hear: quos cum venire rex addidicisset, in fugam vertitur,.
